choices.why: Checking is not charging; without the charge the allowance never runs down.

choices.text: The file's size in megabytes, multiplied by the sheet's price
choices.why: Bytes are in none of the units a picture is billed in.

prompt: Marketing wants the phone line to speak in a well-known presenter's voice, cloned from TV clips. What does lesson 6 say?
hint: Multimodal AI: Image, Audio and Video, lesson 6.

choices.text: Not without the presenter's consent; the shop needs no clone
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is fine as long as the line says the voice is synthetic
choices.why: Saying it is a machine is owed to the caller; it does not replace the presenter's consent.

choices.text: It is fine once the cloning model's card shows an open licence
choices.why: A model's licence covers the model, not putting words in somebody's mouth.

choices.text: It is fine, since clips aired on public TV are public material
choices.why: A recording being public does not make the voice anybody's to use.

prompt: A three-hour meeting is transcribed in pieces cut at silences rather than as one large upload. Besides fitting under 25 MB, what do the pieces buy?
hint: Multimodal AI: Image, Audio and Video, lesson 10.

choices.text: Context across each cut, which a single long upload of the whole meeting would lose
choices.why: It is the other way round: pieces lose the context across a cut.

choices.text: A lower price, since short files are billed less per second
choices.why: Transcription is billed by the second whatever the file.

choices.text: A failed request costs one piece, and pieces go out at the same time
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Segment times that need no adjusting afterwards
choices.why: Each piece is timed from its own start; its offset has to be added back.

prompt: Your MIT-licensed repository ships a Piper voice whose model card points to a research dataset's licence page. What does your MIT licence cover?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 18.

choices.text: Your own code; what the voice allows is set by its dataset's terms
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Everything in the repository, voice included, since you chose the licence
choices.why: You cannot relicense somebody else's model or the data it was trained on.

choices.text: Nothing, since one part of the repository carries research terms
choices.why: Your code is still yours to license; the voice keeps its own terms beside it.

choices.text: The voice too, once its author is credited in the README
choices.why: A credit does not change what the dataset's licence allows.

prompt: Week four of six, and your AI project's plan still has: an evaluation set with results before and after, a streaming chat page, a fallback to a second provider, and accounts. Which is never on the cutting list?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 6.

choices.text: The streaming chat page, since a reviewer tries it before anything else
choices.why: A reviewer of AI engineering looks past the chat screen, for the evaluation.

choices.text: The evaluation set, which is this project's one thing
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The fallback, since a demo that goes down looks broken
choices.why: A fallback multiplies the work and can wait under not yet.

choices.text: Accounts, since a public demo needs a sign-in
choices.why: A login is rarely the point, and it stops a reviewer opening the project.

prompt: Which sentence gives your two minutes about an AI project its trade-off?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 19.

choices.text: A higher floor made answers cheaper, and five real questions lost theirs
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Customers asked about standard delivery and got answers about express
choices.why: That is the problem, the part that opens the two minutes.

choices.text: I chose to refuse below a similarity floor rather than let the model guess
choices.why: That is the decision; the trade-off is what it cost.

choices.text: On 42 test questions it now answers 23 and refuses the rest in one agreed sentence
choices.why: That is the result, which ends on something the listener can open.

prompt: Your AI project's tests run on every push. Some check its rules in code; the evaluation calls a paid model. What belongs on every push?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 12.

choices.text: Everything, since a test that runs only some of the time is a test that stops running
choices.why: The paid run would bill every README edit; it is triggered by what can change a reply.

choices.text: Only the evaluation, since rules in code rarely break
choices.why: The rules are where a failure would be wrong rather than merely visible.

choices.text: Nothing; the evaluation is run by hand before each release
choices.why: A check somebody has to remember is the one that does not run on the day it matters.

choices.text: Tests that call no model; the paid run waits for reply-changing edits
choices.why: Right.

prompt: After the evaluation, what does somebody hiring a junior AI engineer look for in your project? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 3.

choices.text: Cost and latency, measured rather than guessed
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: What the application does when the model's answer is wrong or malformed
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: How natural the chat screen feels
choices.why: The lesson says it plainly for this track: not the chat screen.

choices.text: Every framework and model the project names
choices.why: Tools are the nouns of an advert; a reviewer opens what the work needs.

prompt: Your project's regression report showed a candidate 48% cheaper and seven times faster, and you want that number on your CV. What happens when the interviewer asks how?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 4.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong: it was measured on a fixed set, so it is an honest number
choices.why: Measured, yes; compared with what shows it was cheaper because it answered less.

choices.text: It came from refusing more: the line describes a worse assistant
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is fine as long as the line says the team did it
choices.why: Whose it was is one question; the problem is what the number is made of.

choices.text: It is fine once rounded to 50%, which reads as an estimate
choices.why: Rounding changes nothing about where the saving came from.

prompt: Your take-home note on an e-mail classifier needs one decision with its cost. Which line is it?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 13.

choices.text: Built with Python, the OpenAI SDK and the jsonschema package, all pinned in requirements.txt
choices.why: A list of tools is not a decision, and it has no cost in it.

choices.text: One retry with the schema's reasons, at the price of a second call now and then
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Sorry that the confidence scores are not finished; I ran out of time on the last evening
choices.why: An apology; what is missing goes in the line about more time.

choices.text: With more time I would add an evaluation set of real e-mails
choices.why: That is the note's third part, what you would do with more time.

prompt: A recruiter opens the screening call with: tell me about yourself. Put your two minutes in the order lesson 11 gives them.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 11.
items: What you do
The evidence
What you are looking for
trap: It is told the way the portfolio course told a project: what you do and the evidence first, and only then what you want.

prompt: In a live exercise you write a function that decides whether a model's reply is a valid ticket, and the plain version works. What does lesson 12 do next?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 12.

choices.text: Rewrite it as the elegant version before the time runs out
choices.why: Improving comes after testing, and only if there is time.

choices.text: Test it aloud on a normal reply and an edge case
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Check it in silence, so as not to interrupt the interviewer
choices.why: The interviewer can only see the thinking you say out loud.

choices.text: Ask the interviewer whether it is correct
choices.why: Testing it is the step; asking replaces showing how you check your own work.
